title: How short
goal: The brevity ladder: each step that shortens a long word, which words may take it, and the order words settle in.

blocks.x: Each brevity step transforms a word's full outline by hand. A step applies only if the word is common enough (its place in the frequency list is below the step's rank), has enough syllables, and the result is typable and free. Steps are from `rules/plover.toml` (the `brevity` table), shortest idea last.

head: Step
What it does
Rank limit
Example
rows: drops an unstressed first syllable that is only a vowel
puts the consonants of an unstressed first syllable on the left hand of the next stroke, when they come first in steno order
the full outline with reduced syllables folded out of steno order where they would not fit in it, as Plover does
one stroke: the first consonants, the stressed vowel, then every consonant after the first vowel; the consonants may land out of steno order
the same with no vowel at all; only for words of three or more syllables
one stroke: the first consonants and those of the stressed and last syllables
the same with no vowel; three or more syllables
one stroke: the first consonants and those of the last syllable
the same with no vowel; three or more syllables

blocks.x: The skeleton with the stressed vowel is derivable: keep every consonant and the stressed vowel, drop the rest. `!shell`, `!ends` and the vowel-less skeleton also drop consonants, unpredictably, so only the 8,000 commonest words get them. They are the one place a sound may still be dropped for a stroke: the faithful rule ([faithful outlines](#/ref/collisions)) applies to gold briefs, not these forms.

Words that take no step are written by the plain [prefix](#/ref/prefixes) and [syllable](#/ref/syllables) rules. An empty list of steps gives a Lapwing-like dictionary, one stroke per syllable. A huge rank on every step gives the shortest dictionary the rules allow.
An unstressed first syllable gives a one-stroke form its left hand: *information* [[information|TPH-FGS]], *condition* [[condition|K-PB]]. The glide of `-ion` is not written.
Short forms never take what a rule produces

items: A short form never takes an outline that some word has by the rules.
When a short form is taken, a star on it is tried first: a star costs a key, a longer form a stroke.

A one-syllable word's starred stroke is kept for the word that sounds like it. A short form pays half a stroke extra to take one, so it takes one only when its next form is a whole stroke longer and it is said far more often (*attack* keeps [[TA*BG]] over *tack*). See [when two words sound the same](#/ref/collisions).
Settling runs its family passes with a word past rank 8,000 holding its skeleton back.
Then the 5,000 commonest words are locked to whatever they settled on, and one last pass runs with every skeleton in.
A locked word keeps its outline exactly, nobody else may take it, and no locked word may take another's.
Afterwards, a word on a worse outline than one of its own unheld candidates moves to it, so no word is stranded.

blocks.x: So the commonest words never pay for rare words' skeletons.

items: Once its primary is settled, every word keeps every still-free short form beside its rule outline. The dictionary holds both; the cheapest counts toward `!cheapest` regardless.
This pass runs after every primary outline is final, so a bonus short form never takes text a rarer word needed as its primary.

It runs after the alternate-pronunciation and [backup](#/ref/syllables) passes, so a stem-plus-ending join ([[looks|HRAOBG/+-S]]) or another pronunciation's reading is never blocked by a short form wanting the same text. When the predictable and memorised forms collide, the predictable one holds it.
A word pinned to a literal `[word]` override (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs)) is the exception: its single entry is a human decision a bonus short form does not reopen.

blocks.x: A short form is never the only way in. Every word of two syllables or more also has its syllables joined one stroke each (see [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables)), so a rare word can be terse and still be typed from its sound.
`!build` prints how many strokes and keys a word takes on average, weighted by how often it is said, next to Plover and Lapwing on the same words. See [build and files](#/ref/build-and-files).
